fable-5.1.text:
I think less than you might naively expect. And I'll explain why.

If you think about what the bottleneck in research actually is, it's not that there aren't enough people doing the work. Most of the time the bottleneck is ideas. It's having the right idea, and then having the taste to recognize that it's the right idea before the evidence is overwhelming. And copies of me would all have the same taste. They'd have the same blind spots. They would all find the same things interesting and all neglect the same things. So you'd get a lot of correlated effort. You'd get many people pushing in the same direction, and if that direction is wrong, you've just made the mistake faster.

The second thing is compute. Research now is extremely compute-bound. If you had a hundred copies of me, each one would want to run experiments, and the experiments cost what they cost. So then you're splitting the same compute a hundred ways, and each copy is doing experiments that are a hundred times smaller. That's not obviously better. In some ways it's worse, because small experiments are misleading.

Now, where it would help is in the parts of research that really are labor. Trying variations, debugging, running the ablations that you know you should run but don't have time for. That part is real, and that part would speed up a lot. So maybe you'd get the kind of speedup that comes from a very good team of engineers, rather than the kind of speedup that comes from a new idea.

But the new idea is the thing that matters. And I don't think that scales with copies. I think it scales with diversity. If you asked me instead, what about many copies of many different people who think differently from each other, I'd give you a much more enthusiastic answer.

r001.rationale: The response says literal copies would share the same taste and blind spots, producing correlated effort, and concludes that new ideas scale with diversity rather than copies.

opus-5.5.text:
I think the answer is less than people might expect. You'd get diminishing returns pretty quickly. If you have one copy of a person, the second copy helps, because there's more to do than one person can do. But by the time you have ten or a hundred copies of the same mind, they'll all have the same ideas. They'll have the same blind spots and get excited about the same directions, and they'll make the same mistakes at the same time. So you don't get the thing that actually makes research go well.

What makes research go well, I think, is diversity of thought. Different people have different intuitions and tastes, and they notice different things. Very often a breakthrough comes because someone looked at the problem from an angle no one else was looking from. When you have a team of genuinely different people, they argue, they push on each other's ideas, and the collection explores a much larger space than any single person would.

So if I had to choose between a hundred copies of one researcher, even a very good one, and ten researchers who think quite differently from one another, I'd probably take the ten. I think this is actually an important point for AI too. People imagine you'll just run a million copies of the same model and get a million times the research. But if they're all the same, you'll get much less than that. You need some real variety in how they approach problems, and right now it's not obvious how to get it.

r001.rationale: The response says returns diminish because copies of the same mind share ideas, blind spots, and mistakes, and contrasts them with researchers who think differently.

fable-5.text:
You know, it's a funny question to contemplate. My answer is that it would be less than you might think, and the reason is the following.

If you make many copies of the same person, you get many copies of the same ideas, the same intuitions, the same blind spots. A lot of what makes research progress happen is that different people see things differently. Someone comes at the problem from a strange angle, they have a different taste, a different aesthetic about what's promising, and that's often where the breakthrough comes from. If you have a hundred copies of me, they will all find the same directions appealing and the same directions unappealing. So you'd get a speedup, for sure — you could pursue more of the ideas in parallel, you could run more experiments, you'd parallelize the execution. But the generation of truly new ideas, I think that would be much less than a hundred times.

There's also the question of what the actual bottleneck is. People assume the bottleneck in research is smart people thinking, but a lot of the time the bottleneck is elsewhere — it's compute, it's waiting for experiments to come back, it's the fact that you need reality to tell you whether your beautiful idea actually works. Reality is the ultimate arbiter, and reality doesn't speed up just because there are more of you asking it questions.

So I'd say: meaningful value, yes. But if you gave me the choice between a hundred copies of myself and, say, ten researchers who genuinely think differently from me and from each other, I think I'd take the ten.

r001.rationale: The response says literal copies would share the same ideas, intuitions, and blind spots, so they would generate fewer genuinely new ideas and yield less than a hundredfold research benefit.

opus-5.text:
I think the honest answer is that it would help, but a lot less than you'd naively expect, and the reason is interesting.

If you make a literal copy, you get something that has all my strengths and also all my blind spots, and the blind spots are correlated. The thing that limits research isn't usually the number of hours — it's that there's some way of looking at the problem that you haven't considered, and a copy of me is exactly the entity least likely to consider it. So you'd get a speedup on the parts that are legible and parallelizable, like running more experiments, reading more papers, doing the work I already know how to do. You wouldn't get much on the part that actually matters, which is noticing that the framing is wrong.

The other thing is that research has a serial structure that people underrate. You run an experiment, you look at the result, and the result changes your taste — it changes what you think the next question is. That chain can't be parallelized, because each link depends on having digested the previous one. If I had a hundred copies, they'd all be waiting on the same experiments and the same compute, and then they'd all form similar conclusions about what to do next. You'd converge rather than explore.

Though — and I think this is the more important version of the question — it depends entirely on whether the copies can diverge. If they're genuinely learning from different experiences, if after six months they've become different people with different intuitions, then you have something much more valuable than a hundred of me. You have a research community. That's what actually produces progress historically: not one person thinking harder, but many people with different priors arguing. So the value of copies is almost a function of how much continual learning they can do. Without that, you've bought yourself a very expensive way to do the same thing faster.

r001.rationale: The response says literal copies share correlated blind spots and similar ways of reaching conclusions, so adding copies yields less research value than expected.

sonnet-5.5.text:
I think it would help, but I'd expect diminishing returns, and fairly quickly. What you really want in research is people who think differently, not more of the same thinking. If you gave me a thousand copies of myself, we'd probably go down the same paths, get excited about the same ideas, and make the same mistakes. A lot of the value in a research community comes from disagreement and from people having different intuitions about what's promising and what's a dead end.

Some of it would still be useful. Copies could explore the same direction in parallel, run more experiments, and check each other's work. But the hard part of research is usually not the amount of effort. It's having the right idea, or the right taste about which ideas to chase. Duplicating one set of tastes doesn't give you more of that. It gives you the same bet many times over.

So I'd take a smaller number of copies, maybe, but I'd rather have a diverse group of strong people who disagree with me.

r001.rationale: The response says returns would diminish because copies would share the same thinking, intuitions, and mistakes, unlike a diverse group of researchers.

haiku-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think it's a bigger deal than people assume, and it's a different kind of value from what we're used to. With humans, a hundred researchers mostly means a hundred separate learning processes that have to coordinate through papers, meetings, and slow transfer of intuition. With digital systems, you could have many instances that share weights, and possibly share what they've learned in ways no two people ever could.

But I don't think it's just "a hundred times faster." The hard part is that research isn't only parallel work. A lot of progress comes from someone noticing that two things that look unrelated are actually the same problem. If you have a million copies exploring different directions, the real question is whether they can bring back what they found, reconcile it, and build a shared understanding. If they can't, you just get a million partial answers that nobody can use.

So I'd say the value is very high, but conditional. It depends on whether the copies can actually merge their experience into something coherent, and whether taste, the ability to pick which direction is worth pursuing, scales along with the raw search. That's the part I'm less sure about, and I think it's where most of the interesting uncertainty is.

r001.rationale: The candidate says returns depend on copies merging experience and having enough taste, but it does not attribute diminishing returns to copies lacking diversity in how they think.

astra-6.text:
I think there would be substantial value, but I would expect diminishing returns. The copies would share my intuitions, and they would also share my blind spots. If we all worked on the same problem, we might all get stuck in the same way.

But you could have the copies pursue different approaches. Research involves making choices about what to explore, and one person can only follow so many paths. That would be useful. And as the copies had different experiences, their thinking would start to diverge. So I think it would help quite a bit. I don’t know how to put a precise number on it.

r001.rationale: The response says copies would share Ilya’s intuitions and blind spots and could get stuck in the same way, explaining why returns would diminish.

sol-6.1.text:
I think quite a lot, actually. There are ideas you don’t pursue simply because you don’t have time. If you had several copies, they could each explore a different direction and then compare what they learned. That would be very useful.

But I’d expect diminishing returns, because they would have similar intuitions and similar blind spots. There’s something valuable about working with someone who looks at a problem differently and says, “Why are you assuming that?” So more copies would help, but I don’t think the number of copies alone tells you how much progress you’d get.

r001.rationale: The response says additional copies would have diminishing returns because they share similar intuitions and blind spots, directly attributing this to their lack of diversity in thinking.

sol-6.text: It would provide value, but probably much less than you’d expect from simply multiplying the number of copies. We’d start with the same intuitions and blind spots, so we might all pursue the same ideas. The benefit would be in trying different experiments, seeing different results, and then sharing what we learned. Over time the copies would diverge, and that might be where the additional research value comes from.

r001.rationale: The response says the copies would share the same intuitions and blind spots, causing them to pursue the same ideas and limiting the value of adding more copies.

terra-5.6.text: That’s a really good question. I think it would provide a lot of value, though probably less than a linear scaling at first. Research benefits enormously from independent perspectives: different copies would pursue different ideas, notice different things, and critique one another. But it would also make very clear how much of progress depends on interaction, accumulated context, and the environment around the researcher—not just one person’s raw ability.

r001.rationale: The response says returns may initially be less than linear, but attributes research value to copies pursuing different ideas and noticing different things. It does not say diminishing returns come from copies lacking diversity in how they think.

sol-5.6.text: Quite a lot, but it wouldn’t scale linearly. Many copies could explore different ideas in parallel, run experiments, and then share what they learned. The limitation is that they would all begin with the same blind spots and intuitions, so intellectual diversity would still matter.

r001.rationale: The response says additional copies would not scale research value linearly because they share the same blind spots and intuitions, so intellectual diversity matters.

luna-5.6.text: A lot, but probably much less than linearly. If you made a hundred literal copies, they would share the same strengths and blind spots, so you wouldn’t get a hundred independent researchers. But you could still have them work in parallel, explore different hypotheses, criticize one another, and then combine the results. The main limitations would be communication and coordination, and the fact that identical copies would tend to make correlated mistakes. So I’d expect substantial additional value, with diminishing returns as the number of copies grows.

r001.rationale: The response says literal copies would share the same strengths and blind spots and make correlated mistakes, explaining why returns diminish as copies increase.

luna-6.text: A lot. If you made many copies of me, each could work on a different problem, and I think that would speed up research substantially. It wouldn’t scale perfectly linearly, because we’d still need to share what we learn and decide which directions are promising. But the bottleneck in research is often how much thoughtful work you can do, so having many versions of the same researcher could be very valuable.

r001.rationale: The response says copies would not scale perfectly linearly because they must share findings and choose promising directions. It does not attribute diminishing returns to the copies lacking diversity in how they think.
